chapter.title: Sorting items down two belts

cards.body: What should happen to the one email out of 30 that says 'urgent'? Nothing, unless you say so. On your assembly line every item rides the same belt past the same stations, so you add a **sorting gate**: one station that looks at one thing on each item and pushes it down one of two belts.
cards.simpler: What should happen to the one email out of 30 that says 'urgent'? Nothing, unless you tell it to. Your workflow is like an assembly line. Every item rides the same belt past the same stations. So you add a **sorting gate**. It is one station that looks at one thing on each item and pushes it down one of two belts.

cards.prompt: Your line pulls in 30 support emails. One subject line says 'URGENT: checkout is down'. There's no sorting station yet. What happens to that email?

options.text: n8n spots the word and moves it to the front of the queue.
It rides the same belt as the other 29 and gets exactly the same treatment.
The workflow pauses and asks you what to do with it.

whyNot.a: That's a person reading the subject, not a workflow: n8n only notices what a station tells it to check.
whyNot.c: That's a person checking in, not an assembly line: with no sorting station, nothing makes the belt stop or ask.

cards.reteach: A workflow has no opinions. Every item goes past every station in order until a station tells it to go somewhere else. Without a sorting gate, the urgent email and the newsletter get handled exactly the same way.

cards.title: One question, two exits
cards.body:
The IF node asks one yes-or-no question about each item. That question is called a *condition*: does the subject contain 'urgent'?

On the right side of the box are two exits, labelled true and false. Think of a parcel depot with one chute splitting in two. **Every item leaves by one exit or the other**, and you plug a different station into each.

You build the condition in three parts: the field to check, the test (*contains*, *is equal to*), and the value. *One small catch: 'Urgent' and 'urgent' look different to n8n unless you switch on Ignore Case.*
cards.simpler: The IF node asks one yes-or-no question about each item, called a condition: does the subject contain 'urgent'? It has two exits, true and false, like a parcel chute that splits in two. **Every item leaves by one exit or the other**, and each exit feeds a different station. A condition has three parts: the field, the test (contains, is equal to), and the value. One catch: n8n sees 'Urgent' and 'urgent' as different unless you turn on Ignore Case.

cards.title: The snapped chain
cards.body: Priya handles repair bookings for a small bike shop, and every booking form lands in n8n. She adds an IF node: is the field urgency equal to 'Today'? On Monday 14 bookings come in. After the run, the canvas shows **2 items on the true belt**, which pings the mechanic in Slack, and 12 on the false belt, which go into a Google Sheet for later in the week. The mechanic now hears about the snapped chain before the customer has to phone twice.
cards.simpler: Priya takes repair bookings for a bike shop. Each booking lands in n8n. She adds an IF node that asks: is urgency equal to 'Today'? On Monday, 14 bookings arrive. After the run, the canvas shows **2 items on the true belt**. Those ping the mechanic in Slack. The other 12 go down the false belt into a Google Sheet for later in the week. The mechanic hears about the snapped chain before the customer has to call twice.

cards.prompt: Each invoice has a field called status. You want the overdue ones emailed to finance and every other invoice added to a sheet. Which setup does that?

options.text: IF node: status is equal to 'overdue'. True belt goes to Gmail, false belt goes to Google Sheets.
IF node: status is equal to 'overdue'. Gmail and Google Sheets both on the true belt.
Filter node keeping only 'overdue', then Gmail, then Google Sheets.

whyNot.b: That's one belt doing both jobs, not two belts: the paid invoices go out the false exit and land nowhere.
whyNot.c: That's the Filter, not the IF: it throws away every invoice that isn't overdue, so the sheet never sees them.

cards.reteach: Ask what each pile needs. Overdue invoices need an email, and the rest need a row in a sheet. Two piles with two jobs means two belts, so use the IF node and plug one station into each exit.

cards.title: A bin instead of a belt
cards.body:
Sometimes the 'no' pile doesn't need a second belt. It needs a bin. The Filter node uses the same kind of condition but has only one exit. Items that pass carry on. Items that fail are dropped, like a sorter at the post office tossing junk mail before it reaches the bags.

You'd think throwing data away is risky. For noise, it's a relief. Out-of-office replies and newsletters need nothing done to them.

Here's the rule: **if the 'no' items still need a job, use IF.** If they need nothing, use Filter.
cards.simpler: Sometimes the 'no' pile needs a bin, not a second belt. The Filter node runs the same kind of check but has only one exit. Items that pass carry on. Items that fail are dropped, like a post office sorter tossing junk mail. Dropping data sounds risky, but for noise it's a relief. Out-of-office replies and newsletters need nothing done. The rule: **if the 'no' items still need a job, use IF.** If they need nothing, use Filter.

cards.body: Tom wants urgent emails posted in Slack, so he adds a Filter for 'urgent' and plugs in Slack. It works perfectly. Three weeks later a colleague asks why the inbox log stopped getting the normal emails. They'd been dropped at the Filter since the day he built it. The way to spot it: after a test run, **count what leaves the station**. If items that still needed a job aren't on any belt, you wanted an IF.
cards.simpler: Tom wants urgent emails posted in Slack. He adds a Filter for 'urgent' and connects Slack. It works perfectly. Three weeks later, a colleague asks why the inbox log stopped getting normal emails. The Filter had been dropping them since the day he built it. How to catch this: after a test run, **count what leaves the station**. If items that still needed a job aren't on any belt, you needed an IF.

cards.prompt: Which sentence describes the IF node, not the Filter node?

options.text: Every item leaves by one of two exits, true or false.
Items that fail the check are dropped and go nowhere.
It reads each email and decides for itself what counts as urgent.

whyNot.b: That's the Filter, not the IF: the Filter has one exit and a bin, while the IF keeps both piles moving.
whyNot.c: That's guessing, not a condition: n8n only runs the exact test you write, like 'subject contains urgent'.

cards.reteach: Picture the IF node as a fork in the belt. Nothing falls off. Every item takes the true road or the false road, decided by one test you wrote. The Filter is the one with a bin.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
An IF node checks one field on each item and sends it down a true belt or a false belt, so urgent and normal things get different jobs. **A Filter uses the same check but drops whatever fails**, so only use it when the 'no' pile needs nothing done.

Tomorrow: when a station jams, n8n marks it in red. Here's how to read it.
cards.simpler: An IF node checks one field on each item and sends it down a true belt or a false belt. That way urgent and normal things get different jobs. **A Filter uses the same check but drops whatever fails**, so use it only when the 'no' pile needs nothing done. Tomorrow: when a station jams, n8n marks it in red, and you'll learn how to read it.

cards.body: Open the workflow from last chapter. Add an IF node just before the final app step, check one field for one word, and run it once. Then read the two belts: how many items went true, and how many went false?
cards.simpler: Open the workflow you built last chapter. Add an IF node just before the final app step. Have it check one field for one word, then run it once. Now **read the two belts**: how many items went down true, and how many went down false?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now send items down two different belts based on one field's value, and drop the ones that need nothing.
